title: Caring for Others
description: Ten portraits of people who care for others: nurses, volunteers, foster parents, counselors, ambulance workers, teachers and doctors.

lessons.title: The Night Nurse
lessons.summary: A night nurse moves through the quiet hours of a hospital ward, caring for patients until morning.
lessons.text:
Rosa has worked the night shift on a hospital ward for eleven years, and she has learned that a hospital night has its own shape. It begins with a surge of activity and ends, on a good night, in a long, quiet stretch before dawn.

When Rosa arrives at seven in the evening, she puts on the sensible shoes that she wears for every shift: soft, flat and plain. They are not pretty, but after twelve hours on her feet, sensible shoes are the difference between a sore back and a good sleep.

Between seven and ten there is a surge of tasks: medicines to give, families to talk to, new patients arriving from the emergency department. Visitors may stay until nine; after that, visits are prohibited, except for the close family of very sick patients. Rosa explains the rule gently, because nobody likes to hear that something is prohibited, especially when they are worried about someone.

By midnight, the ward has grown quiet. Most patients are asleep, and the lights in the corridor are turned down to a faint yellow glow. In that faint light, Rosa walks from room to room with a portable monitor, a small machine that she can carry to any bed to check a patient's heart rate and blood pressure. Because the portable monitor is light and easy to move, she rarely has to wake anyone to use it.

Some people imagine that the night shift is dull, and some moments are: forms to complete, supplies to count. But Rosa has never found the work itself dull, because night is when patients often feel most alone. An old man in room 6 cannot sleep, so she brings him a glass of water with an ice cube in it, the way he likes it, and sits with him for a few minutes. He tells her that one cube is perfect and two is too many, and they both smile.

A teenage girl in room 9 is listening to music through her headphones. When Rosa comes in, the girl takes off her headphones and asks quietly whether her operation tomorrow will hurt. Rosa answers honestly and kindly. Afterward, the girl puts her headphones back on, calmer than before.

Rosa keeps a few handy things in her pockets: a pen, a small light, tape and tissues. The tissues are especially handy at night, when worries seem larger than they are.

At about four, she finally drinks a cup of coffee and, as usual, spills a little on her sleeve. The brown stain will not come out until she washes the uniform at home. One of her colleagues laughs and says that a coffee stain is the badge of every night nurse.

At seven in the morning, Rosa gives her report to the day team and walks out into the early light, tired but content.

Questions:
How does a night on the ward begin and end?
It begins with a surge of activity and ends in a quiet stretch before dawn.
Why does Rosa wear sensible shoes?
After twelve hours on her feet, sensible shoes protect her back.
What does Rosa use to check patients without waking them?
She uses a portable monitor, which is light and easy to move.
What does the old man in room 6 like?
He likes a glass of water with one ice cube in it.
What does Rosa's colleague say about the coffee stain?
The colleague says that a coffee stain is the badge of every night nurse.

lessons.title: What the Last Weeks Teach
lessons.summary: A volunteer reflects on what she has learned from sitting with people at the end of their lives.
lessons.text:
Every Tuesday afternoon, I spend three hours at a hospice, a small house where people who are near the end of their lives are cared for. I am not a nurse or a doctor, and I have no medical training whatsoever. My job is simpler: I make tea, I read to people and I listen. When I began, four years ago, I was uncertain whether I could do it, and uncertain what to say to someone who was dying.

What I have learned is that the words matter less than I thought. Most of the people I visit want no advice whatsoever. They want company, and they want to be seen as the people they have always been, not only as patients.

There was Walter, a retired bus driver, who taught me to play poker. He had played poker with the same three friends for forty years, and when they could no longer visit, he taught me instead. We played for buttons, not money.

There was Helen, a former music teacher, who could no longer speak much but could still sing. She would sing a melody without words, and I would try to guess the song. Once I recognized the melody, an old folk tune, and sang a few lines with her, and she held my hand with surprising strength. That moment of affection between two people who barely knew each other is something I still think about. I had not expected so much affection in such a place.

Some patients want to tell their story. One man had always meant to write a memoir about his childhood on a farm, and in his last months, he told it to me, chapter by chapter, while I typed. It was not a famous life, and no one will ever write his biography. But a biography is someone else's account of a life, while a memoir is your own, and it mattered to him that his story was told in his own voice. His daughter has printed his memoir for his grandchildren.

Is the work sad? At times, it is. But much of what worries us in ordinary life becomes irrelevant in that house. Whether a colleague was rude, what other people think of our clothes: all of it seems irrelevant beside someone in their final weeks. What remains is love, honesty and kindness.

The French writer Montaigne, following the old Greek and Roman philosophers, wrote that to study philosophy is to learn how to die. I am no philosopher, but I think that the hospice has taught me something close to that. It has taught me to live with a clearer conscience. I apologize sooner now, and I thank people more often. On Tuesday evenings, I drive home with a lighter conscience.

I do not know how many more years I will volunteer, but those three hours are the most honest hours of my week.

Questions:
What does the writer do at the hospice?
The writer makes tea, reads to people and listens.
How did the writer feel when she began?
The writer was uncertain whether she could do it.
What did Walter teach the writer?
He taught the writer to play poker, and they played for buttons, not money.
What is the difference between a memoir and a biography?
A biography is someone else's account of a life, while a memoir is your own.
Why does the writer drive home with a lighter conscience?
The writer apologizes sooner and thanks people more often.

lessons.title: My Mother's Songs
lessons.summary: A daughter describes caring for her mother, whose memory is fading, with photographs and music.
lessons.text:
For three years now, I have been caring for my mother, Elena, who has a disease that slowly damages the memory. She lives with my husband and me.

The disease does not take memories in a neat order. Recent events go first: what she ate for lunch, whether she has taken her pills, the name of the new nurse. Older memories stay intact much longer. She may not remember that I visited her an hour ago, but her memories of childhood are almost perfectly intact: the white house in her village, the smell of her mother's bread, the blue sea below the hill.

Greece is her homeland, and as the present grows obscure to her, her homeland grows clearer. She left as a young woman, on a long voyage by ship to New York, and she can still describe that voyage in detail: the storms and the first sight of the city lights. Some days the recent past is so obscure to her that she asks for her own mother, who died long ago. On those days, I have learned not to argue. Instead, I ask her to tell me about her homeland, and she relaxes.

Last winter, I found her old photographs scattered across the bottom of a closet, in no order at all. Over many afternoons, we sorted the scattered pictures together and used glue to fix them into a large album. She enjoyed the work: spreading the glue, pressing each photo down and writing a name beneath it when she could. The album is now the most useful object in our house. When she is confused, we open it, and the faces help her find her way.

Music helps even more. A nurse told me that songs are often stored differently in the brain, and that a familiar melody can act as a cue, bringing back memories that seemed lost. So I made a list of the songs of her youth, the soundtrack of her life, from village dances to the radio hits of her first years in this country. When I play that soundtrack in the evening, she sings along, and the words come back to her as if no time had passed. Each song is a cue for a different memory: one brings back her wedding, another her first job in a shop.

Evening is the hardest time. As the light turns amber and the shadows grow long, she sometimes becomes anxious and desperately wants to "go home." In those moments, I hold her hand, we sit together in the amber light, and I play her favorite song. At first, I wanted desperately to bring her memory back. Now I want something simpler: for her to feel safe.

She does not always know my name. But she always knows that she is loved, and that, I think, is what matters most.

Questions:
Which memories stay intact longest?
Her older memories, especially of her childhood, stay intact much longer than recent ones.
How did Elena come to New York?
She came on a long voyage by ship as a young woman.
What did the writer and her mother do with the scattered photographs?
They sorted them and used glue to fix them into a large album.
Why does music help Elena?
A familiar melody can act as a cue that brings back memories that seemed lost.
What does the writer want for her mother now?
The writer wants her mother to feel safe.

lessons.title: A Room for Marcus
lessons.summary: A teenage boy slowly settles into life with his foster parents.
lessons.text:
When Marcus, a boy of 14, came to live with Ruth and David Park, he arrived with one bag of clothes and a box of comic books. Ruth and David had been foster parents for six years, and they knew that the first days are rarely easy.

For the first week, Marcus barely spoke. He stayed in his room reading manga, comic books from Japan that are read from right to left. David, who had never read manga, asked him how it worked. Marcus said very little, but the next day he left one of his books on the kitchen table, and David read it from cover to cover. That evening, they talked about it for twenty minutes, their longest conversation so far.

Marcus also loved superhero films. His favorite superhero was not the strongest one, but the one who had lost his family and kept going anyway. Ruth understood why that mattered to him.

Food helped too. When Ruth asked what he liked to eat, Marcus said quietly that his grandmother used to make red bean soup. Ruth found a recipe and cooked a large pot of bean soup on Sunday. Marcus said it was not quite like his grandmother's, but he ate two bowls.

Not everything was easy. In the second month, Marcus came home three hours late without calling. Ruth and David were very worried, and when he finally walked in, David was furious. He was not furious because a rule had been broken, but because he had been afraid. Once he had calmed down, he told Marcus exactly that. Marcus was quiet for a long time. Then he said that nobody had ever worried about him before.

A social worker explained later that this kind of rebellion is common. A child who has been moved from home to home may test new parents, half expecting to be sent away again. The rebellion, she said, is often really a question: will you still keep me? Ruth and David answered it in the only way they could: by staying calm and by staying.

David, who knew nothing about video games, decided to learn the one Marcus played. Marcus explained that the gameplay of his favorite game was less about fighting than about building a city. David was terrible at it, but the gameplay gave them something to share every evening.

Marcus had a younger sister, Ana, who lived with another foster family two hours away. Hoping to see her felt risky to him, because his hopes had been disappointed before. Ruth understood that, for Marcus, even hope was a risky thing.

In the spring, the social workers arranged a reunion. Ruth drove Marcus to a park halfway between the two homes. When Ana saw her brother, she ran across the grass and almost knocked him over. The reunion lasted only two hours, but Marcus talked about it for weeks. Now the two families meet once a month, and each reunion is a little easier than the last.

Questions:
What did Marcus read in his room?
He read manga, comic books from Japan that are read from right to left.
Why was David furious when Marcus came home late?
He was furious because he had been afraid.
What did the social worker say about the rebellion?
She said it is often really a question: will you still keep me?
Where did the reunion with Ana take place?
It took place in a park halfway between the two homes.

lessons.title: The Counselor's Door
lessons.summary: A high school counselor explains how she notices, listens and helps students plan their future.
lessons.text:
The door of Maria Lopez's office is almost always open. Maria has been a counselor at a large public high school for fifteen years, and she says that the open door is the most important part of her job.

People often think that a school counselor only helps students choose their classes. "That is part of it," Maria says, "but a large part of my work is simply noticing." If a happy student becomes quiet, or a good student starts to be absent from class, she wants to know why. A student who is absent once is probably sick. A student who is absent every Monday may be dealing with something at home.

The hardest question in her work, she says, is when to intervene. If she intervenes too early, students feel watched and stop trusting her. If she waits too long, a small problem may have become a large one. Usually, she begins with an ordinary conversation, and she listens far more than she talks. She will only intervene directly, by calling parents or outside services, when a student's safety is at risk.

Ten years ago, most conflicts between students happened in the halls. Today, many of them happen on phones. Every new class now takes a short cyber safety course, in which students learn how to protect their privacy online and what to do when they are treated badly there. Maria helped to design the cyber safety course herself.

Older students worry most about college. Tuition has risen quickly, and many families find it hard to manage financially. Part of Maria's work is to explain that tuition is not the whole story: there are scholarships, grants and cheaper community colleges. A family that is struggling financially can often still find a way. Every fall, colleges visit the school, recruiting students. Some recruiting visits are helpful; others feel like advertising, and Maria helps students see the difference.

What makes a strong college application? Maria's answer is honesty. The most compelling essays, she says, are rarely about great achievements. They are about something real: caring for a younger brother, working in a family shop. She reads many first drafts, and she always suggests revision. "A first draft is a beginning," she tells students. After two or three rounds of revision, a student's own voice usually comes through, and the essay becomes compelling.

Does she dislike anything about the job? Maria will concede that the admin side is tiring: forms, reports and schedules. Some weeks she spends more hours on admin than with students. But she will also concede that the forms matter, because they help make sure that no student is forgotten.

Why does she stay? Because, she says, a single conversation can change the direction of a life. Former students who come back to visit rarely remember her advice. What they remember is that her door was open.

Questions:
What does Maria say is a large part of her work?
She says that a large part of her work is simply noticing.
When does Maria intervene directly?
She intervenes directly only when a student's safety is at risk.
What do students learn in the cyber safety course?
They learn how to protect their privacy online and what to do when they are treated badly.
What makes a college essay compelling, according to Maria?
The most compelling essays are honest and about something real.
What does Maria concede about the admin side of the job?
She concedes that it is tiring, but also that the forms matter.

lessons.title: Calm Is the Main Tool
lessons.summary: An ambulance worker explains the routine that helps him stay calm in emergencies.
lessons.text:
James Okafor has worked on an ambulance for twelve years. If you ask him what the most important tool in his job is, he will not name a machine. "Calm," he says. "Everything else is equipment."

His station sits on the fringe of the city, near the airport, where the last houses give way to warehouses and fields. From the station's windows, he can watch the planes landing on the runway. Each landing, he points out, follows a careful routine. An ambulance call, in his view, should work in the same way.

The routine begins before any emergency. At the start of each shift, James and his partner check the ambulance from top to bottom: the oxygen, the medicines, the bed, even the wheels. He runs his hand along the rim of each wheel to make sure that nothing is damaged, because a bent rim can cause trouble on a fast drive. Many of the medicines they carry are strictly regulated by law, so each one must be counted, signed for and locked away. "Medicines are regulated for good reasons," he says.

The city also plans the deployment of its ambulances with care. Instead of waiting only at stations, some ambulances wait at busy points around the city, such as a major intersection, so that they can reach more people quickly. The deployment changes during the day: in the morning, more ambulances wait near the highways; late at night, more wait near the city center.

Halfway through the shift, a call comes in. A woman has had a seizure outside a shop near a busy intersection. As they drive, James explains what a seizure is: a short burst of unusual electrical activity in the brain. Most seizures stop on their own within a few minutes. The most helpful thing that people nearby can do is to keep the person safe from hard objects, note the time and wait for help.

When the ambulance arrives, the seizure has already stopped. The woman is awake but confused. James sits down beside her, tells her his name and explains, slowly and clearly, where she is and what happened. He knows that calm is catching: if he is calm, she will become calmer too.

Good delegation is integral to every call. James leads, and he gives each person one clear task. His partner checks the woman's blood pressure; a police officer keeps the crowd back; a shop worker brings a coat for her shoulders. "Delegation is not about giving orders," he says. "It is about making sure that nobody is wondering what to do."

Communication with the hospital is integral as well. On the way, James calls ahead, so that a team is ready when they arrive. By evening, the woman is resting at home.

Back at the station, James makes a cup of tea and watches another plane come down onto the runway.

Questions:
Where is James's station?
It sits on the fringe of the city, near the airport.
Why does James check the rim of each wheel?
A bent rim can cause trouble on a fast drive.
How does the city plan the deployment of its ambulances?
Some ambulances wait at busy points, such as a major intersection, and the deployment changes during the day.
What is a seizure, according to James?
It is a short burst of unusual electrical activity in the brain.
Why is delegation integral to every call?
It makes sure that nobody is wondering what to do.

lessons.title: The Doctor in the Highlands
lessons.summary: A profile of a children's doctor who runs a small clinic in a mountain region.
lessons.text:
The road climbs for an hour through pine forests before it reaches the village of San Rafael, at an elevation of about 2,000 meters. At that elevation, the air is thin and cool, even in summer, and in winter the road is sometimes closed by snow for days. Here, Dr. Lucia Mendes has worked as a children's doctor for nine years.

Dr. Mendes grew up in a large city. She first came to the highland region as a young doctor, for what she expected to be one year. She stayed because she fell in love with the place and because, as she puts it, "the children here needed a doctor more than the city did." Today, her clinic serves about four thousand people across the highland villages.

The clinic belongs to the local municipality, which covers six villages and many scattered farms. The municipality pays for the building and two nurses; the rest of the budget comes from the region and from donations. Money is always short, so Dr. Mendes has learned to be practical. She and three other rural clinics buy their medicines wholesale, together, which lowers the cost considerably. Buying wholesale was her idea, and it saves the clinics thousands of dollars a year.

Electricity was once a serious problem. Storms often cut the power line, and a clinic without power cannot keep medicines cold. Five years ago, with help from the municipality, the clinic installed solar panels and batteries. The renewable power is not only cheaper; it is also more reliable. "Renewable energy sounds like a political subject," she says, "but for us it simply means that the vaccines stay cold."

Her work follows the seasons. In winter, she treats coughs and fevers. In summer, many families take seasonal work on farms in the lower valleys, and she travels to visit their children there. She plans her year around this seasonal pattern.

Autumn brings its own task. Many families in the region pick wild mushrooms, a tradition that goes back generations. Most are delicious, but a few are dangerous, especially for small children. Every September, Dr. Mendes gives a talk at the village school about which mushroom is safe and which is not, and she reminds parents never to let children eat a mushroom they have found without asking an adult.

She is careful, she says, never to overlook small things. A child who seems merely tired may have a problem with her blood; a quiet boy may have trouble hearing. In a small place, a doctor who knows every family is less likely to overlook such signs, because she remembers how each child usually behaves.

The window of her office overlooks the whole valley. On clear mornings, she can see the villages she serves along the river. "Some people think working here means giving something up," she says. "I think I have gained much more than I have given."

Questions:
At what elevation is the village of San Rafael?
It is at an elevation of about 2,000 meters.
Why did Dr. Mendes stay in the highland region?
She fell in love with the place, and the children there needed a doctor.
Why does the clinic buy medicines wholesale?
Buying wholesale, together with other clinics, lowers the cost.
What does renewable energy mean for the clinic?
It means that the power is more reliable and the vaccines stay cold.
What does Dr. Mendes teach at the school every September?
She teaches which mushroom is safe and which is not.

lessons.title: The School on the Fourth Floor
lessons.summary: A teacher at a hospital school brings science to life for children who must stay in the hospital.
lessons.text:
Most people do not know that many children's hospitals have their own schools. Children who must stay in the hospital for weeks or months still need to learn, and they need, perhaps even more, the ordinary feeling of going to class. Nora Bell has taught at the school of a large children's hospital for seven years.

Her classroom is on the fourth floor, directly under a glass dome at the top of the building. On sunny days, light pours down through the dome and fills the room. Students who cannot leave their beds have their lessons in their rooms.

Her students are of every age, and each one follows a different plan. One morning, she may teach reading to a seven-year-old and the atomic structure of matter to a teenager. She explains that atomic science begins with the simplest atom of all, hydrogen. A hydrogen atom has just one proton at its center and one electron moving around it. Last month, her student Leo, who is twelve, built a model of a hydrogen atom from a small ball and a piece of wire, and it now hangs above the window. Leo has since asked to learn about every atomic model in the textbook.

Another student, Maya, loves computers. Nora taught her that computers store information in binary code, using only two numbers, zero and one. At first, binary seemed strange to Maya, but soon she was writing her name in binary on the board. Together, they built a simple bot, a small robot on wheels, and Maya programmed the bot to move across the table and stop at the edge. The hospital's tablets were not compatible with the program they needed, so a volunteer found two older laptops that were compatible with it.

Not every lesson stays inside the room. Once a month, Nora arranges a video call with a scientist or traveler. In the spring, the class met an ocean explorer who studies a coral reef in the Pacific. The explorer took the children on a virtual dive, showing them the colors of the reef and the fish that live among its corals. She explained that a reef is built very slowly by tiny animals, over thousands of years. For children who had not been outside for weeks, the reef felt like a different planet.

After the call, a quiet girl who rarely spoke asked whether she, too, could become an explorer one day. The explorer answered at once: "Of course you can. Every explorer begins by asking questions."

Nora believes that school in the hospital is not about keeping up with tests. It is about reminding children that they are still students, still curious and still growing, even when they are sick. As the light falls through the glass dome in the afternoon, she can often see that reminder working.

Questions:
Where is Nora's classroom?
It is on the fourth floor, directly under a glass dome.
What is a hydrogen atom made of?
It has one proton at its center and one electron moving around it.
How do computers store information in binary?
They use only two numbers, zero and one.
Why did a volunteer find two older laptops?
The hospital's tablets were not compatible with the program, but the laptops were.
What did the ocean explorer show the children?
She showed them the colors of a coral reef and the fish that live among its corals.

lessons.title: The Professor's Stories
lessons.summary: A home care worker helps a retired historian recover from knee surgery and listens to his stories.
lessons.text:
Three mornings a week, Grace Owens visits Professor Arthur Wells, a retired historian of 86 who lives alone in a narrow house full of books. Grace is a home care worker. Since Arthur had a knee reconstruction in March, an operation to rebuild the damaged joint, she has helped him with the things he cannot yet do alone: washing, cooking, shopping and, above all, walking.

On each visit, they practice the exercises his doctor has given him. The knee reconstruction went well, but recovery is slow, and Arthur is not a patient man. To keep him going, Grace has found a simple method: she asks him questions about history. As long as he is talking, he forgets to complain.

Arthur spent forty years studying the royal families of Europe, and he can talk about them for hours. He explains that, for centuries, the death of a sovereign was a dangerous moment for a country. If a sovereign left no clear heir, the question of succession could divide the nobles and even lead to war. "The rules of succession," he says, "were really rules for keeping the peace." He tells her that the same problem appeared in many parts of the world. After the death of the Prophet Muhammad, for example, his followers had to decide who should lead them, and each leader they chose received the title of caliph. Arguments over who should be the next caliph shaped history for centuries.

On the shelf above his chair stands a small wooden model of a royal carriage, painted gold. Arthur likes to explain that a sovereign rode in such a carriage to be seen by the people, because a ruler who was never seen was soon forgotten. Grace dusts the carriage every week.

His favorite subject, however, is not kings at all. His last book was about a siege: a small city that was surrounded by an army for seven months, four hundred years ago. During the siege, the people shared their food, cared for the sick and kept the city's bread ovens burning until the last sack of flour. After the siege ended, they spent twenty years on the reconstruction of their homes and churches. In Arthur's book, ordinary people always come to the fore: bakers, nurses, children. "Kings are in every history book," he says. "I wanted to bring the others to the fore."

In June, Arthur turned 87. His doctor had told him to avoid alcoholic drinks while he was taking his pain medicine, so Grace brought a bottle of apple juice instead. "No alcoholic drinks, but we can still celebrate," she said.

By the end of the summer, Arthur could walk to the corner and back alone. He told Grace that she had been an excellent student. Grace laughed and told him that he had been a difficult patient, but a wonderful teacher.

Questions:
Why does Grace help Arthur?
He had a knee reconstruction and cannot yet do everything alone.
How does Grace keep Arthur walking?
She asks him questions about history.
Why was the death of a sovereign dangerous?
If there was no clear heir, the question of succession could divide the nobles and even lead to war.
What did the people of the city do during the siege?
They shared their food, cared for the sick and kept the bread ovens burning.
Why did Grace bring apple juice?
Arthur's doctor had told him to avoid alcoholic drinks while he was taking his pain medicine.

lessons.title: The Rescue at the Swamp
lessons.summary: A volunteer at a wildlife center helps a duck and a fox recover and return to the wild.
lessons.text:
Caring for others does not always mean caring for people. On weekends, Sofia Reyes volunteers at a small wildlife rescue center on the edge of a large swamp. The center takes in injured birds and animals, treats them and, whenever possible, returns them to the wild.

The swamp is a rich and busy place. Birds with long legs stand in the shallow water, turtles rest on fallen trees, and in spring the air is full of song. It is also a place where people fish, which causes many of the injuries that Sofia sees. Some people leave old fishing lines, hooks and bait behind them. Birds are attracted by the bait, swallow it or become caught in the line, and cannot free themselves.

One Saturday in April, a walker called the center to report a duck that was struggling near the bank. Sofia and the center's vet, Dr. Hale, drove out with a net and a carrier. The bird was a drake, a male duck, with a bright green head and a white ring around his neck. Fishing line was wrapped around one of his legs. To reach him, Sofia had to step into the swamp, and the water came up to her waist. She moved slowly, so that she would not scare him, and caught the drake gently in the net.

Back at the center, Dr. Hale carefully cut away the line. The drake's leg was swollen but not broken. For a week he stayed in a quiet pen, and Sofia fed him and checked his leg every day. By the following Saturday, he was swimming in the center's pond as if nothing had happened.

The center's other patient that month was a young fox. A farmer had found her near his barn, unable to run. She was lame, and when Dr. Hale examined her, he found that one of her hind legs had been hurt, probably by a fence. The fox was lame for nearly three weeks. Sofia learned to bring her food without making eye contact, because wild animals feel safest when they are not watched. Slowly, the fox began to put weight on her hind leg again, and then to run around her pen.

Sofia also spends part of each weekend on a less exciting task: cleaning the paths along the swamp. With other volunteers, she collects old lines, hooks and bait, and the center has placed signs asking people who fish to take their things home. Prevention, Dr. Hale says, is the best medicine.

At the end of May, they returned both patients to the wild on the same day. The drake flew low over the water and landed among a group of other ducks. The fox ran into the tall grass at the edge of the swamp, stopped once to look back and then disappeared. Sofia stood at the bank, wet up to her waist again, and felt that her weekends had never been better spent.

Questions:
Where is the wildlife rescue center?
It is on the edge of a large swamp.
Why are many birds injured at the swamp?
Some people leave old fishing lines, hooks and bait, and birds become caught or swallow the bait.
What is a drake?
A drake is a male duck.
How deep was the water when Sofia caught the drake?
The water came up to her waist.
Why was the fox lame?
One of her hind legs had been hurt, probably by a fence.
